headline: 34% of UK open data states no licence at all
detail: Without a stated licence you cannot know whether you may republish, build on, or sell work using the data. We count a licence recorded anywhere the publisher put it, including the non-standard fields data.gov.uk uses — this is after that recovery, not before it.
sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM datasets d WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM duplicates x WHERE x.key = d.key) AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM retired r WHERE r.key = d.key) AND d.license_norm IS NULL
post: 34% of the UK's open data doesn't say what licence it's under. Not 'restrictive' — unstated. You cannot legally know whether you may reuse 28,026 datasets. https://open-data.org.uk

headline: 3 datasets published by councils that no longer exist now lead nowhere
detail: 43 English councils were abolished in the 2019-2023 reorganisations. We hold 1,098 datasets published in their names. Of the 1,079 whose links we have followed, 3 (0%) are dead — the catalogue entry survived the council, the server didn't. Nobody inherited the duty to move the data. The list stops at 2019, so this is a floor.
post: When a council is abolished its data dies with it. We hold 1,098 datasets from 43 councils abolished since 2019 — 0% of the links we've followed are dead. The records are still listed. They just don't go anywhere. https://open-data.org.uk

headline: 5 of 296 councils in England leave no trace in the UK's open data at all
detail: Checked against the ONS register of local authorities. These councils have no datasets under their own name and are not named in anybody else's either — not their own site, not data.gov.uk, not a regional portal. A further 15 in England appear only inside another publisher's records, usually a national geoportal: their data exists but cannot be attributed to them, which is a finding about attribution rather than about the council. Councils with no trace: Bournemouth, Christchurch and Poole, Folkestone and Hythe, Mid Devon, West Northamptonshire, Westmorland and Furness
sql: council_coverage.json state=='none', minus councils named in another publisher's titles or descriptions
post: 5 of 296 councils in England leave no trace in the UK's open data — nothing under their name anywhere. Method: https://open-data.org.uk/about

headline: 3,045 dataset links point at 28 servers that no longer answer
detail: Across 138 publishers. Each hostname was tried from two separate networks and failed from both — either it no longer resolves at all, or it resolves and nothing is listening. Hosts that merely refused our checker are excluded, as are 22 that turned out to answer perfectly well, which were our own error rather than anyone's dead server. The catalogue entries are all still listed.
sql: scripts/dead_hosts.py — connection failures grouped by host, re-probed
post: 3,045 links in the UK's open data catalogues point at servers that don't answer any more — 28 hostnames across 138 public bodies. Every record still sits there looking perfectly healthy. https://open-data.org.uk

headline: 99 councils published their INSPIRE data through one address, and that address stopped answering
detail: 894 datasets from 99 different councils all resolve to inspire.misoportal.com, which does not respond from any network we tried. The parent domain is alive and the supplier is still trading — it is this endpoint that went. Councils met a statutory publishing duty by pointing at a shared service, and when the address changed nobody went back to update 99 catalogues. No single portal could notice this: each one holds a handful of records that look fine.

councils: Borough Council of King's Lynn and West Norfolk

sql: dead_hosts.json — the host serving the most distinct publishers
post: 99 UK councils published their INSPIRE data through a single shared address. It stopped answering. 894 datasets now lead nowhere and every catalogue still lists them as available. https://open-data.org.uk

headline: "Conservation Areas" is published by 102 bodies under 17 different licences
detail: The same kind of dataset, produced for the same statutory reason, released on terms that differ by council — and some on no stated terms at all. Anyone wanting a national picture has to reconcile 17 licences first; 16 of the 108 copies state none.
sql: same normalised title, >= 10 publishers, >= 3 distinct licences
post: 102 public bodies publish "conservation areas". Between them they use 17 different licences and 16 state none at all. Same data, same duty, 17 sets of rules. https://open-data.org.uk/who-publishes

headline: Service Personnel and Veterans Agency states no licence on 100% of its datasets
detail: Measured across publishers holding at least 100 datasets. This states what the catalogue records, not whether the data is in fact reusable — the publisher may intend it to be.
post: Service Personnel and Veterans Agency publishes 114 datasets and states no licence on 114 of them (100%). Nobody can legally reuse what they can't identify the terms of. https://open-data.org.uk

headline: 86% of Marine Management Organisation's dataset links are broken
detail: We follow every resource link and record the response. 'Broken' means a 404, a server error, or a connection that failed — never a server that merely refused our checker, which we record separately as unverified. Two groups are excluded and counted separately: councils abolished since 2019, because a defunct body can't fix its links, and publishers whose whole hosting domain has gone, because that is a decommissioned portal rather than rot.

others.publisher: City of Bradford Metropolitan District Council

sql: availability = 'dead', min 50 checked per publisher, still-existing bodies
post: We followed 352 of Marine Management Organisation's dataset links. 303 are dead — 404s and server errors, not blocks. 86% of what they publish leads nowhere. https://open-data.org.uk
